role: Executive Director, South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department
stance_basis: two letters explicitly stating the S.C. Wildlife and Marine Resources Department opposes construction of the project
summary: James A. Timmerman, Jr., Executive Director of the South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department, submitted multiple letters opposing the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project. His concerns centered on the destruction of trout streams, threats to the two-story trout fishery in Lake Jocassee, disruption of a unique spawning run in Howard Creek, inadequate data to support conclusions in the DEIS, and poor land use practices by Duke Power Company. He requested a delay in licensing and stated opposition unless additional information resolved the uncertainties.
complaint_summary: Timmerman details concerns about destruction of trout streams, threats to Lake Jocassee's two-story fishery, disruption of Howard Creek's spawning run, inadequate data underlying DEIS conclusions, poor land use practices by Duke Power, and formally opposes the project while requesting a delay in licensing.

statement.text:
With this letter, I would like to advise the Pederal Power Commission that the South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department is very concerned over the possible consequences of the construction of the proposed Bad Creek Pump Storage Project by Duke Power Company. The earlier construction of Lake Jocassee by Duke Power Company resulted in the loss of nearly one-fourth of the trout streams in our State. The construction of the proposed Bad Creek Project will destroy additional trout waters, it will damage others for a minimum period of 10-12 years and it will possibly endanger the two story trout fishery that has been established in Lake Jocassee. This is a very serious proposal in South Carolina since this State has a very limited amount of suitable trout habitat remaining.
Upon reviewing the <u>Draft Environmental Impact Statement</u> for <u>Bad Creek Project No. 2740 - South Carolina</u> by Federal Power Commission, Bureau of Power, it is our belief that conclusions have been reached that are based on inadequate information in the light of new facts that have come to the attention of the South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department.
In reviewing temperature and oxygen data collected by the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service for Lakes Keowee and Jocassee for the period 1973 through 1975, observations have been made which have not been addressed, to our knowledge, by the Federal Power Commission in its draft statement. These data indicate that trout habitat in Lake Jocassee is being reduced during the critical months of August, September, and early October (see attached graphs). Whether this reduction in habitat is resulting from Duke Power Company operations, natural phenomena, or a combination of both cannot be determined adequately from the information available at present. It is known, however, that water temperatures in Lake Keowee have risen over time and that the thermocline in Lake Keowee has been altered drastically. Each year warmer water is being exchanged with Lake Jocassee during the pump back operation of the Jocassee Station. This warmer water and the mixing of water by the pump back operation has resulted in a decrease in trout habitat during the critical months of August, September, and October.
Revised Sections 3.1.2.3, 3.2.2.3, and 9 discuss these impacts.
No comment required.
See revised Sections 2.2.2.2 and 3.2.2.3.

Mr. Kenneth P. Plumb March 25, 1976 Page 2
In the case of the proposed Bad Creek Project, conclusions are based on a complex salt water model that may or may not reflect what will occur to trout habitat in Lake Jocassee. Although initial field investigations have tended to support the model, any firm conclusions concerning the effects on trout habitat in Lake Jocassee from related projects are premature. Too much is at stake to speculate that these projects may not damage the two story fishery in Lake Jocassee. This excellent fishery represents the only acceptable compensation for the loss of nearly one-fourth of the trout streams in this State to the construction of Lake Jocassee.
No comment required.
We have had a number of discussions with Duke Power Company's environmental staff concerning the anticipated effects of this project. It should be stressed, however, that the data which is available to support conclusions concerning the probable environmental repercussions of this project are meager. Lake Jocassee was filling during 1973. This leaves only one year of record on which to base the decision. With Duke Power approaching the project from a standpoint of "what should not happen" and our Department attempting to anticipate "what might happen", it is easy to have differing interpretations with just one year's data available.
Insofar as is possible with the available data, Staff has indicated the possible impact of operation of this project in Section 3.2.2.3.
For example, Duke Power Company's biologists appear to feel that the limited data only allows one to make statements concerning trout habitat in the main body of the Lake and reach one conclusion. We feel that we should attempt to use available data to evaluate changes in trout habitat for the entire body of water and reach another conclusion. The only way to determine which interpretations are correct is to develop a better data base. As such, we recommend that the Federal Power Commission delay its liscensing decision until this fall. This would provide an additional year of record for the critical months of August, September, and October.
No comment required.
Another very important fact that has been documented by this department, by Duke Power Company biologists and by the S. C. Chapter of Trout Unlimited, but has not been considered by the Federal Power Commission, is a large spawning run of both brown and rainbow trout that is now occurring in Howard Creek below the proposed project. Both ripe and spent brown and rainbow trout have been observed on redds. These fish are migrating from Take Jocassee into Howard Creek to spawn. This has been confirmed by the fact that the ripe and spent trout collected in Howard Creek were marked two years earlier and stocked in Lake Jocassee. As of this date, Howard Creek is the only tributary in South Carolina which receives a spawning run of trout, a unique and highly desirable feature. As you are aware, the construction of the Bad Creek Project would disrupt this large spawning run occurring in Howard Creek for a minimum period of eight to twelve years. It has been suggested that spawning runs may occur in other tributaries; however, this is not known at this time and no information is available as to the probable magnitude, hatching success, etc.
See revised Sections 2.2.2.2 and 3.1.2.3.

Mr. Kenneth P. Plumb March 25, 1976 Page 3
There is also some question as to whether or not Howard Creek could be restored to a suitable quality for trout reproduction after construction. Project plans presently include provisions for flow augmentation. Although it is not known whether flow augmentation will be feasible after construction, necessary capacity to allow for augmentation should be maintained in the project design.
Provisions for flow augmentation are discussed in Sections 3.2.2.2, 4.1 and 9.2.
Another element of concern regarding the proposed project involves the general project area. There is an absence of adequate land use practices by Duke Power Company in relation to the protection of trout streams in the project area. As pointed out in the Draft Environmental Impact Statement, the high turbidities and accumulation of silt and sand found in streams in this area are attributed to erosion from areas disturbed by the construction of numerous roads, logging operations, and geological explorations. This has led to a general degradation over time of trout streams in the project area. Bad Creek, for example, was once a cool, clear stream harboring a good trout population. As a result of poor land use practices, it has now become degraded extensively. Our personnel have found little evidence of any attempt by Duke Power Company to prevent damage to trout streams while conducting their preliminary operations relative to the Bad Creek Project. Areas where geological explorations were conducted are eroding badly, depositing heavy loads of silt and sand into Bad Creek and Howard Creek. No evidence could be found of any attempt to prevent such damage to these streams by Duke Power Company. Duke Power Company should be required to develop and make available for discussion a detailed sedimentation control plan for the general project area.
See revised Sections 2.2.2.2, 3.1.2.2, and 4.
The Wildlife and Marine Resources Department recognizes the need to develop power resources both within our State and the region. In many cases, our Department has offered no opposition to such development but where the development of natural resources results in the loss of critical and irreplaceable natural resources, this Department must stand in opposition. With the considerable uncertainty surrounding this proposed project and the importance of the resources endangered by the project, the South Carolina Wildlife and Marine Resources Department opposes the construction of this project.
